newsitem.title: JORDAN: Chirac wins over Jordan's Islamist deputies.
newsitem.headline: Chirac wins over Jordan's Islamist deputies.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac won rare praise for a Western leader from Jordanian Islamists on Thursday after warning of humanitarian disaster in Iraq and calling for greater understanding between Islam and the West.

They said Chirac, who addressed Jordanian parliamentarians during his visit to Amman on Thursday, offered more balanced policies towards the Middle East than the United States, seen by Arabs as biased towards Israel.

"We support a more assertive role for Europe...and France is leading this role," said leading Islamist deputy Bassam al-Amoush after hearing Chirac speak. "This brings to the fore another group and destroys the hegemony of the U.S. over our region."
Chirac, who visited Israel and the Palestinian self-rule territories before arriving in Jordan, has called for a greater European role in the Middle East peace process.
Chirac's campaign ran into serious opposition during his visit to Israel, but has been well received in the Arab world.

Speaking in the same parliamentary chamber boycotted by Islamists two years ago when U.S. President Bill Clinton visited for the signing of Jordan's peace treaty with Israel, Chirac repeated his call for the Palestinians right to their own state.

"The Israelis have not been accustomed to see a Western leader who tries to be even handed," said Hamza Mansour, spokesman of the Islamic Action Front (IAF), Jordan's largest political grouping. "They have seen the Western leadership
always biased towards them and so when they see a Western leader steeering away from the circle of Zionist pressures they are upset," he added.
In his speech to the Jordanian parliament, Chirac appealed to the international community to carry out "at long last" a deal allowing Iraq to sell some oil to buy food and medicine.
His comments prompted long applause from the deputies.
Amoush said Chirac's appeal struck a positive chord with Jordanians sympathetic to the suffering of Iraq's civilian population.
"The speech had positive elements as regards the human attitude towards the plight of the Iraqi people and his position on the holy sites and his stress on a Palestinian state," said Amoush.

Citing Jordan as a model of tolerance, Chirac devoted much of his Amman speech to the relationship between Islam and the West, dramatised by last year's wave of bombings by suspected Algerian Moslem extremists in France.

The French leader praised Islam as a religion of moderation and attributed the rise of "extremist movements that divert Islam to serve violence" as a result of economic and social change that had produced frustration and exclusion.
"We must reject the action of those who legitimate recourse to violence and who build artificial frontiers between Islam and the West," Chirac said.
"Islam rejects extremism but most cases that are called extremism are reactions to extremism of states and governments and the injustice coming from European, Western and local states," said Mansour.
Amoush, however said Jordan's Islamists, who have been vocal opponents of the Middle East peace accords, differed fundamentally with Chirac over the right of Israel to exist.

"We differ with Chirac on his view on the recognition of the state of Israel and we in the Islamic Action Front do not recognise the Zionist entity because it is a transient entity and the rightful owners, the Palestinians, exist," he said.
